arXiv:2609.39218v1 [math.AC] 30 Sep 2026

ARITHMETIC PSEUDO-FROBENIUS NUMBERS AND DETERMINANTAL NUMERICAL SEMIGROUP RINGS

DO VAN KIEN Address: Department of Mathematics, Hanoi Pedagogical University 2, Xuan Hoa, Phu Tho, Vietnam Email address: dovankien@hpu2.edu.vn
Abstract.

Let H=⟨a1,…,an⟩H=\langle a_{1},\ldots,a_{n}\rangle be a numerical semigroup. A conjecture on numerical semigroup rings predicts that the defining ideal IHI_{H} has a determinantal presentation if and only if the set of pseudo-Frobenius numbers of HH has form {h+α,h+2​α,…,h+(n−1)​α}\{h+\alpha,h+2\alpha,\ldots,h+(n-1)\alpha\} for h≥0,α>0h\geq 0,\alpha>0. We prove this conjecture under the condition that hh has a unique factorization in HH. We also give characterization this unique-factorization condition. As an application, we consider the family of affine-orbit numerical semigroups determined by m=c​An−1+1m=cA_{n-1}+1, 1≤c≤a1\leq c\leq a. We prove that the relevant element hh has a unique factorization and obtain

IH=I2⁡(X1ax2a⋯Xn−1aXncX2x3⋯XnX1d+c+1−a).I_{H}=\operatorname{I}_{2}\begin{pmatrix}X_{1}^{a}&x_{2}^{a}&\cdots&X_{n-1}^{a}&X_{n}^{c}\\ X_{2}&x_{3}&\cdots&X_{n}&X_{1}^{d+c+1-a}\end{pmatrix}.

In particular, the Eagon–Northcott complex of the matrix mentioned above gives the graded minimal free resolution of k⁡[H]k[H].

Key words and phrases: 
Numerical semigroup, Pseudo-Frobenius number, Defining ideal, Determinantal ideal, Affine map, Eagon–Northcott complex
2020 Mathematics Subject Classification
Primary 13D02; Secondary 13A02, 20M25

1. Introduction

Let H=⟨a1,…,an⟩H=\langle a_{1},\ldots,a_{n}\rangle be a numerical semigroup minimally generated by n≥3n\geq 3 positive integers, and let k⁡[H]=k⁡[ta1,…,tan]k[H]=k[t^{a_{1}},\ldots,t^{a_{n}}] be its semigroup ring over a field kk. Let S=k⁡[X1,…,Xn]S=k[X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}] be the weighted polynomial ring with deg⁡Xi=ai\deg X_{i}=a_{i} for every 1≤i≤n1\leq i\leq n and consider the graded kk-algebra homomorphism φ:S⟶k⁡[H]\varphi:S\longrightarrow k[H] given by φ⁡(Xi)=tai\varphi(X_{i})=t^{a_{i}} for all ii. The ideal IH=Ker⁡φI_{H}=\operatorname{Ker}\varphi is called the defining ideal of the numerical semigroup ring k⁡[H]k[H]. Determining the structure of IHI_{H} is a classical problem in the study of monomial curves and numerical semigroup rings. There are a few known results about the structure of IHI_{H}. The most important result is due to J. Herzog [11] when n=3n=3, but for semigroups with more generators, the situation becomes significantly more complex. When n=4n=4, there are some partial answers to describe the structure of the defining ideal: e.g. symmetric semigroups ([3]), pseudo-symmetric semigroups ([14]), and almost symmetric semigroups ([7]). For n(≥4)n(\geq 4)-generated cases, research has primarily focused on specific classes, such as those generated by arithmetic sequences [8] or repunit numbers [2, 16], making a comprehensive understanding still unattainable.

In general, explicitly determining IHI_{H} presents substantial difficulty, even when its numerical invariants have been established. A particularly useful numerical invariant is the set of pseudo-Frobenius numbers

PF⁡(H)={f∈ℤ∖H∣f+s∈H​ for every ​0<s∈H}.\operatorname{PF}(H)=\{f\in\mathbb{Z}\setminus H\mid f+s\in H\text{ for every }0<s\in H\}.

These numbers determine the degrees of the minimal generators of the canonical module of k⁡[H]k[H]; in particular, the Cohen-Macaulay type r⁡(k⁡[H])\rm{r}(k[H]) of k⁡[H]k[H] is equal to ♯​PF⁡(H)\sharp\operatorname{PF}(H) (see [10]). Motivated by the interaction between pseudo-Frobenius numbers and defining ideals established in [9, 12], the following conjecture was formulated by the author together with D. T. Cuong, N. Matsuoka, and H. L Truong (see [13, Conjecture 1.1]).

Conjecture 1.1.

Let H=⟨a1,…,an⟩H=\langle a_{1},\ldots,a_{n}\rangle be minimally generated by n≥3n\geq 3 elements. The following conditions are equivalent.

  1. (1)

    After a suitable permutation of the generators,

    IH=I2⁡(X1ℓ1X2ℓ2⋯XnℓnX2m2X3m3⋯X1m1)I_{H}=\operatorname{I}_{2}\begin{pmatrix}X_{1}^{\ell_{1}}&X_{2}^{\ell_{2}}&\cdots&X_{n}^{\ell_{n}}\\ X_{2}^{m_{2}}&X_{3}^{m_{3}}&\cdots&X_{1}^{m_{1}}\end{pmatrix}

    for some positive integers ℓ1,…,ℓn,m1,…,mn\ell_{1},\ldots,\ell_{n},m_{1},\ldots,m_{n}.

  2. (2)

    There exist h≥0h\geq 0 and α>0\alpha>0 such that

    PF⁡(H)={h+α,h+2​α,…,h+(n−1)​α}.\operatorname{PF}(H)=\{h+\alpha,h+2\alpha,\ldots,h+(n-1)\alpha\}.

Here, I2⁡(M)\operatorname{I}_{2}(M) denotes the ideal of SS generated by 2×22\times 2 minors of a matrix MM whose entries are in SS.

The implication (1)⇒(2)(1)\Rightarrow(2) has already been established in [12]. The converse remains open in general, although it has been proved for several classes, including almost symmetric numerical semigroups [9], numerical semigroups of maximal embedding dimension [12], stretched numerical semigroup rings [13], generalized repunit numerical semigroups [2, 5], and certain families satisfying restrictions involving the multiplicity and the embedding dimension [17].

The main result of this paper gives a general sufficient condition for the converse. Assume that

PF⁡(H)={h+α,h+2​α,…,h+(n−1)​α}.\operatorname{PF}(H)=\{h+\alpha,h+2\alpha,\ldots,h+(n-1)\alpha\}.

For 1≤i≤n1\leq i\leq n, put

mi=min⁡{ℓ>0∣ℓ​ai+α∈H},Mi=mi−1,m_{i}=\min\{\ell>0\mid\ell a_{i}+\alpha\in H\},\,M_{i}=m_{i}-1,

and set

h′=M1​a1+M2​a2+⋯+Mn​an.h^{\prime}=M_{1}a_{1}+M_{2}a_{2}+\cdots+M_{n}a_{n}.

We first show that

Mi=max⁡{qi∣(q1,…,qn)∈𝖹⁡(h)},M_{i}=\max\{q_{i}\mid(q_{1},\ldots,q_{n})\in\mathsf{Z}(h)\},

where 𝖹⁡(h)\mathsf{Z}(h) denotes the set of factorizations of hh. This yields the equivalences

h has a unique factorization⟺h′=h⟺h′+α∉H.h\text{ has a unique factorization}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad h^{\prime}=h\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad h^{\prime}+\alpha\notin H.

Thus a homological problem concerning IHI_{H} is reduced to the factorization of a single element of HH.

The central theorem is the following.

Theorem 1.2 (Theorem 3.7).

Suppose that PF⁡(H)={h+α,h+2​α,…,h+(n−1)​α}\operatorname{PF}(H)=\{h+\alpha,h+2\alpha,\ldots,h+(n-1)\alpha\} and that h=q1​a1+⋯+qn​anh=q_{1}a_{1}+\cdots+q_{n}a_{n} is the unique factorization of hh in HH . Then, after a suitable permutation of a1,…,ana_{1},\ldots,a_{n}, there exist positive integers r1,…,rnr_{1},\ldots,r_{n} such that

(qi+1)​ai+α=ri+1​ai+1,1≤∀i≤n,(q_{i}+1)a_{i}+\alpha=r_{i+1}a_{i+1},1\leq\forall i\leq n,

with indices taken modulo nn. Consequently,

IH=I2⁡(X1q1+1X2q2+1⋯Xnqn+1X2r2X3r3⋯X1r1).I_{H}=\operatorname{I}_{2}\begin{pmatrix}X_{1}^{q_{1}+1}&X_{2}^{q_{2}+1}&\cdots&X_{n}^{q_{n}+1}\\ X_{2}^{r_{2}}&X_{3}^{r_{3}}&\cdots&X_{1}^{r_{1}}\end{pmatrix}.

In particular, the graded minimal SS-free resolution of k⁡[H]k[H] is given by the Eagon–Northcott complex of the matrix mentioned above.

The interesting point is that the unique factorization of hh, together with the arithmetic structure of PF⁡(H)\operatorname{PF}(H), forces the relations

(qi+1)​ai+α∈H(q_{i}+1)a_{i}+\alpha\in H

to form a single directed cycle through all the minimal generators. This produces the cyclic monomial matrix. The case h=0h=0 is compatible with the determinantal situation studied in [9]; the theorem above applies to an arbitrary nonnegative translation hh. In particular, if HH has maximal embedding dimension, we recover the statement [12, Theorem 2 (2)⇒(4)(2)\Rightarrow(4)].

We then apply this criterion to numerical semigroups generated by the orbit of their multiplicity under an affine map. Let a,n,ca,n,c be integers such that a≥2,n≥3,1≤c≤a.a\geq 2,n\geq 3,1\leq c\leq a. For each 1≤i≤n1\leq i\leq n, put Ai=1+a+⋯+ai−1A_{i}=1+a+\cdots+a^{i-1} and m=c​An−1+1m=cA_{n-1}+1. Let bb be an integers such that b≥−(a−2)​m−2b\geq-(a-2)m-2 and gcd⁡(m,b)=1.\gcd(m,b)=1. Let d=(a−1)​m+bd=(a-1)m+b and si=m+d​Ais_{i}=m+dA_{i} for all ii. Consider the numerical semigroup H=⟨s0,s1,…,sn−1⟩H=\left<s_{0},s_{1},\ldots,s_{n-1}\right>, where s0=ms_{0}=m. In [1], Álvarez, Moreno-Ávila and Ojeda determined the pseudo-Frobenius numbers

PF⁡(H)={ρ,ρ−b,…,ρ−(n−2)​b},\operatorname{PF}(H)=\{\rho,\rho-b,\ldots,\rho-(n-2)b\},

where ρ=d⁡(m−1)+(c−1)​m.\rho=d(m-1)+(c-1)m. They also considered the monomial matrix

Xc=(X1aX2a⋯Xn−1aXncX2X3⋯XnX1d+c+1−a)X_{c}=\begin{pmatrix}X_{1}^{a}&X_{2}^{a}&\cdots&X_{n-1}^{a}&X_{n}^{c}\\ X_{2}&X_{3}&\cdots&X_{n}&X_{1}^{d+c+1-a}\end{pmatrix}

and asked whether its 2×22\times 2 minors generate the whole defining ideal; see [1, Remark 8.2].

We answer this question affirmatively. Our proof of the determinantal presentation is independent of their proof of the containment I2⁡(Xc)⊆IH\operatorname{I}_{2}(X_{c})\subseteq I_{H}. Using the weighted-degree criterion of [13, Section 2.3], that containment follows directly from the affine relations among the generators. We then prove that, after writing the above pseudo-Frobenius numbers in increasing order as

PF⁡(H)={h+α,h+2​α,…,h+(n−1)​α},α=|b|,\operatorname{PF}(H)=\{h+\alpha,h+2\alpha,\ldots,h+(n-1)\alpha\},\qquad\alpha=|b|,

the element hh has a unique factorization. Theorem 1.2 therefore yields the reverse containment.

We obtain the following result.

Theorem 1.3 (Theorems 4.3 and 4.4).

Let a≥2a\geq 2, n≥3n\geq 3, 1≤c≤a1\leq c\leq a, A0=0A_{0}=0 and Ai=ai−1a−1A_{i}=\dfrac{a^{i}-1}{a-1} for all 1≤i≤n1\leq i\leq n. Let m=c​An−1+1m=cA_{n-1}+1 and b∈ℤb\in\mathbb{Z} satisfy b≥−(a−2)​m−2b\geq-(a-2)m-2 and gcd⁡(m,b)=1.\gcd(m,b)=1. Put d=(a−1)​m+b,si=m+d​Aid=(a-1)m+b,s_{i}=m+dA_{i}, and H=⟨s0,…,sn−1⟩H=\langle s_{0},\ldots,s_{n-1}\rangle. Then the following statements hold true.

  1. 1)

    PF⁡(H)={h+α,h+2​α,…,h+(n−1)​α}\operatorname{PF}(H)=\{h+\alpha,h+2\alpha,\ldots,h+(n-1)\alpha\} for some h≥0,α>0h\geq 0,\alpha>0.

  2. 2)

    hh has a unique factorization and

    IH=I2⁡(X1aX2a⋯Xn−1aXncX2x3⋯Xnx1d+c+1−a).I_{H}=\operatorname{I}_{2}\begin{pmatrix}X_{1}^{a}&X_{2}^{a}&\cdots&X_{n-1}^{a}&X_{n}^{c}\\ X_{2}&x_{3}&\cdots&X_{n}&x_{1}^{d+c+1-a}\end{pmatrix}.

Consequently, the Eagon–Northcott complex associated to the matrix in above display gives the graded minimal free resolution of k⁡[H]k[H].

For this explicit family, the equality of ideals can also be proved by reducing modulo X1X_{1} and comparing lengths; see Remark 4.5. The application of Theorem 1.2 has a different purpose. The arithmetic pseudo-Frobenius progression and the unique factorization of hh force the relations among the minimal generators to form a single cycle. That cycle determines the exponents of a determinantal matrix, and the theorem then identifies its minors with the defining ideal. Thus the presentation of this family is an instance of a criterion formulated without reference to the orbit parameters a,b,c,ma,b,c,m or to an a priori candidate matrix. The length computation proves the equality for XcX_{c} efficiently, whereas the criterion explains why the pseudo-Frobenius calculation of [1] leads to a determinantal presentation and provides a route for other families with the same arithmetic and factorization properties.

The paper is organized as follows. Section 2 recalls the basic facts on numerical semigroups, pseudo-Frobenius numbers, and the weighted-degree criterion used for binomial relations. Section 3 develops the unique-factorization criterion and proves Theorem 1.2. Section 4 applies it to the affine-closed family and proves Theorem 1.3.

2. Preliminaries

Throughout this paper, let H=⟨a1,…,an⟩H=\langle a_{1},\ldots,a_{n}\rangle be a numerical semigroup minimally generated by a1,…,ana_{1},\ldots,a_{n}. Let kk be a field and R=k⁡[H]=k⁡[ta1,…,tan]R=k[H]=k[t^{a_{1}},\ldots,t^{a_{n}}] associated to HH. Let S=k⁡[X1,…,Xn]S=k[X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}] be the weighted polynomial ring with deg⁡Xi=ai\deg X_{i}=a_{i} for every 1≤i≤n1\leq i\leq n and consider the graded kk-algebra homomorphism φ:S⟶R\varphi:S\longrightarrow R given by φ⁡(Xi)=tai\varphi(X_{i})=t^{a_{i}} for all ii. Recall that the defining ideal IHI_{H} of RR is defined to be the kernel of φ\varphi.

Definition 2.1.

For 0<h∈H0<h\in H, the Apéry set of HH with respect to hh is defined by

Ap⁡(H,h)={a∈H:a−h∉H}.\operatorname{Ap}(H,h)=\{a\in H:a-h\notin H\}.

Equivalently, if

wi=min⁡{a∈H∣a≡i(modh)}​ for ​0≤∀i≤h−1,w_{i}=\min\{a\in H\mid a\equiv i\pmod{h}\}\text{ for }0\leq\forall i\leq h-1,

then

Ap⁡(H,h)={w0=0,w1,…,wh−1}.\operatorname{Ap}(H,h)=\{w_{0}=0,w_{1},\ldots,w_{h-1}\}.
Definition 2.2.

An integer f∈ℤ∖Hf\in\mathbb{Z}\setminus H is called a pseudo-Frobenius number of HH if f+s∈Hf+s\in H for every 0<s∈H0<s\in H. The set of all pseudo-Frobenius numbers is denoted by PF⁡(H)\operatorname{PF}(H).

We recall the following two facts.

Lemma 2.3 ([15, Proposition 2.19(2)]).

For z∈ℤz\in\mathbb{Z}, one has z∉Hz\notin H if and only if there exists f∈PF⁡(H)f\in\operatorname{PF}(H) such that f−z∈Hf-z\in H.

Lemma 2.4 ([15, Proposition 2.20]).

For each 0<h∈H0<h\in H,

PF(H)={a−h∣a∈Ap(H,h),b−a∉H for all b∈Ap(H,h)∖{a}}.\operatorname{PF}(H)=\{a-h\mid a\in\operatorname{Ap}(H,h),\ b-a\notin H\text{ for all }b\in\operatorname{Ap}(H,h)\setminus\{a\}\}.

The following elementary criterion will be used repeatedly. It is the weighted-degree argument of [13, Lemma 2.11 and Corollary 2.12].

Lemma 2.5 (Weighted-degree criterion).

Let the matrix

M=(f1f2⋯fng1g2⋯gn),M=\begin{pmatrix}f_{1}&f_{2}&\cdots&f_{n}\\ g_{1}&g_{2}&\cdots&g_{n}\end{pmatrix},

where fi,gif_{i},g_{i} are monomials of positive degree in SS. Suppose that there exists an integer δ\delta such that deg⁡gi−deg⁡fi=δ\deg g_{i}-\deg f_{i}=\delta for all 1≤i≤n1\leq i\leq n. Then I2⁡(M)⊆IH.\operatorname{I}_{2}(M)\subseteq I_{H}.

Proof.

For 1≤i<j≤n1\leq i<j\leq n, set Δi​j=fi​gj−fj​gi\Delta_{ij}=f_{i}g_{j}-f_{j}g_{i}. By assumption, we have

deg⁡fi+deg⁡gj=deg⁡fi+deg⁡fj+δ=deg⁡fj+deg⁡gi.\deg f_{i}+\deg g_{j}=\deg f_{i}+\deg f_{j}+\delta=\deg f_{j}+\deg g_{i}.

Every monomial u∈Su\in S satisfies φH​(u)=tdeg⁡u\varphi_{H}(u)=t^{\deg u}. Hence φH​(Δi​j)=0\varphi_{H}(\Delta_{ij})=0, so every 2×22\times 2 minor of MM belongs to IHI_{H}. ∎

Remark 2.6.

The integer δ\delta in Lemma 2.5 is not required to be positive. This will be useful in the last section for the affine family when b<0b<0.

3. A unique-factorization criterion for determinantal defining ideals

Throughout this section, let H=⟨a1,…,an⟩,n≥3H=\langle a_{1},\ldots,a_{n}\rangle,n\geq 3, and assume that

(⋆\star) PF⁡(H)={h+α,h+2​α,…,h+(n−1)​α},\operatorname{PF}(H)=\{h+\alpha,h+2\alpha,\ldots,h+(n-1)\alpha\},

where h≥0h\geq 0 and α>0\alpha>0.

Setting 3.1.

For each 1≤i≤n1\leq i\leq n, put mi=min⁡{ℓ>0∣ℓ​ai+α∈H},Mi=mi−1m_{i}=\min\{\ell>0\mid\ell a_{i}+\alpha\in H\},M_{i}=m_{i}-1, and define

h′=M1​a1+M2​a2+⋯+Mn​an.h^{\prime}=M_{1}a_{1}+M_{2}a_{2}+\cdots+M_{n}a_{n}.

We also set

𝖹⁡(h)={(q1,…,qn)∈ℕn∣h=∑i=1nqi​ai}.\mathsf{Z}(h)=\left\{(q_{1},\ldots,q_{n})\in\mathbb{N}^{n}\mid h=\sum_{i=1}^{n}q_{i}a_{i}\right\}.

Let us begin with a basic observation.

Lemma 3.2 ([12, Lemma 2]).

Under the condition (⋆\star), one has h∈Hh\in H and α∉H\alpha\notin H.

Proof.

If α∈H\alpha\in H, then (h+α)+α=h+2​α∈H(h+\alpha)+\alpha=h+2\alpha\in H, because h+α∈PF⁡(H)h+\alpha\in\operatorname{PF}(H), a contradiction. Hence α∉H\alpha\notin H. By Lemma 2.3, there exists 1≤i≤n−11\leq i\leq n-1 such that

h+i​α−α=h+(i−1)​α∈H.h+i\alpha-\alpha=h+(i-1)\alpha\in H.

If i≥2i\geq 2, then h+(i−1)​α∈PF⁡(H)h+(i-1)\alpha\in\operatorname{PF}(H) which is a contradiction. Therefore i=1i=1, and h∈Hh\in H. ∎

Lemma 3.3 (Boundary lemma).

For every c∈Hc\in H, then c+α∉Hc+\alpha\notin H if and only if h−c∈H.h-c\in H.

Proof.

Suppose first that c+α∉Hc+\alpha\notin H. By Lemma 2.3, there exists 1≤i≤n−11\leq i\leq n-1 such that

h+i​α−(c+α)=h+(i−1)​α−c∈H.h+i\alpha-(c+\alpha)=h+(i-1)\alpha-c\in H.

If i≥2i\geq 2, then adding c∈Hc\in H gives h+(i−1)​α∈Hh+(i-1)\alpha\in H, contradicting (⋆\star). Thus i=1i=1, and h−c∈Hh-c\in H.

Conversely, suppose that h−c∈Hh-c\in H and c+α∈Hc+\alpha\in H. Then h+α=(h−c)+(c+α)∈Hh+\alpha=(h-c)+(c+\alpha)\in H, contrary to h+α∈PF⁡(H)h+\alpha\in\operatorname{PF}(H). ∎

Proposition 3.4.

For every ii, we have

Mi=max⁡{qi∣(q1,…,qn)∈𝖹⁡(h)}.M_{i}=\max\{q_{i}\mid(q_{1},\ldots,q_{n})\in\mathsf{Z}(h)\}.
Proof.

By definition, one has Mi​ai+α∉HM_{i}a_{i}+\alpha\notin H and (Mi+1)​ai+α∈H(M_{i}+1)a_{i}+\alpha\in H. Applying Lemma 3.3, we obtain h−Mi​ai∈Hh-M_{i}a_{i}\in H and h−(Mi+1)​ai∉Hh-(M_{i}+1)a_{i}\notin H. Hence MiM_{i} is exactly the maximum possible ii-th coordinate among the factorizations of hh. ∎

Corollary 3.5.

One has h′−h∈Hh^{\prime}-h\in H.

Proof.

Take any factorization h=∑i=1nqi​aih=\mathop{\sum}\limits_{i=1}^{n}q_{i}a_{i} with 0≤qi∈ℤ0\leq q_{i}\in\mathbb{Z} for all ii. We then have by Proposition 3.4 that qi≤Miq_{i}\leq M_{i} for all ii. Therefore

h′−h=∑i=1n(Mi−qi)​ai∈H.h^{\prime}-h=\sum_{i=1}^{n}(M_{i}-q_{i})a_{i}\in H.

∎

Theorem 3.6.

Under (⋆\star), the following statements are equivalent.

  1. 1)

    hh has a unique factorization in HH.

  2. 2)

    h′=hh^{\prime}=h.

  3. 3)

    h′+α∉Hh^{\prime}+\alpha\notin H.

Proof.

Suppose first that h=q1​a1+⋯+qn​anh=q_{1}a_{1}+\cdots+q_{n}a_{n} is the unique factorization of hh. By Proposition 3.4, for each ii there exists a factorization of hh whose ii-th coordinate is MiM_{i}. By uniqueness, this factorization must be the one above. Hence qi=Miq_{i}=M_{i} for all ii, so h=h′h=h^{\prime}.

Conversely, suppose h=h′h=h^{\prime}, and let h=q1​a1+⋯+qn​anh=q_{1}a_{1}+\cdots+q_{n}a_{n} be any factorization. Then we have by Proposition 3.4 that qi≤Miq_{i}\leq M_{i}, and therefore

0=h′−h=∑i=1n(Mi−qi)​ai.0=h^{\prime}-h=\sum_{i=1}^{n}(M_{i}-q_{i})a_{i}.

Since all ai>0a_{i}>0, it follows that qi=Miq_{i}=M_{i} for every ii. Thus the factorization is unique.

Finally, Lemma 3.3, applied to c=h′c=h^{\prime}, gives the equivalence

h′+α∉H⟺h−h′∈H.h^{\prime}+\alpha\notin H\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad h-h^{\prime}\in H.

Moreover, we already know by Corollary 3.5 that h′−h∈Hh^{\prime}-h\in H. Since H⊆ℕH\subseteq\mathbb{N}, both h−h′h-h^{\prime} and h′−hh^{\prime}-h can belong to HH only when h=h′h=h^{\prime}. ∎

We now prove the main result of this section.

Theorem 3.7.

Assume (⋆\star). Suppose h=q1​a1+⋯+qn​anh=q_{1}a_{1}+\cdots+q_{n}a_{n} is the unique factorization of hh. Then, after a suitable permutation of a1,…,ana_{1},\ldots,a_{n}, there exist positive integers r1,…,rnr_{1},\ldots,r_{n} such that

(qi+1)​ai+α=ri+1​ai+1,1≤∀i≤n,(q_{i}+1)a_{i}+\alpha=r_{i+1}a_{i+1},1\leq\forall i\leq n,

where indices are taken modulo nn. Consequently,

IH=I2⁡(X1q1+1X2q2+1⋯Xnqn+1X2r2X3r3⋯X1r1).I_{H}=\operatorname{I}_{2}\begin{pmatrix}X_{1}^{q_{1}+1}&X_{2}^{q_{2}+1}&\cdots&X_{n}^{q_{n}+1}\\ X_{2}^{r_{2}}&X_{3}^{r_{3}}&\cdots&X_{1}^{r_{1}}\end{pmatrix}.

In particular, the graded minimal SS-free resolution of k⁡[H]k[H] is given by the Eagon–Northcott complex [6] of the the matrix mentioned above.

Proof.

Since the factorization of hh is unique, Proposition 3.4 gives qi=Miq_{i}=M_{i} for all ii. Thus qi​ai+α∉Hq_{i}a_{i}+\alpha\notin H and (qi+1)​ai+α∈H(q_{i}+1)a_{i}+\alpha\in H. Put ci=(qi+1)​ai+αc_{i}=(q_{i}+1)a_{i}+\alpha. No factorization of cic_{i} can contain aia_{i}, because subtracting one copy of aia_{i} would imply qi​ai+α∈Hq_{i}a_{i}+\alpha\in H.

For each ii, we define

Ti={j∣ci−aj∈H,1≤j≤n}.T_{i}=\{j\mid c_{i}-a_{j}\in H,1\leq j\leq n\}.

Corollary 3.9 ([12], Theorem 2).

Then (d+c−a)​m=L​m+d​W(d+c-a)m=Lm+dW, so (d+c−a−L)​m=d​W(d+c-a-L)m=dW. Hence, since gcd⁡(m,d)=1\gcd(m,d)=1, there exists t∈ℕt\in\mathbb{N} such that W=t​mW=tm and d+c−a−L=t​dd+c-a-L=td. Thus L=(1−t)​d+c−aL=(1-t)d+c-a.

If t=1t=1, then L=c−a≤0L=c-a\leq 0. When c<ac<a, this is impossible because W=m>0W=m>0; when c=ac=a, one has L=0L=0 while W=m>0W=m>0, again impossible. If t≥2t\geq 2, then L<0L<0, also impossible.

Thus t=0t=0, and hence W=0W=0. We then get x1=⋯=xn−1=0x_{1}=\cdots=x_{n-1}=0 and x0=d+c−ax_{0}=d+c-a so that h=(d+c−a)​s0h=(d+c-a)s_{0} is the unique factorization as desired. ∎

Combining the two cases yields the following.

Theorem 4.3.

Under the hypotheses above, write (4.1) in increasing order as

PF⁡(H)={h+α,h+2​α,…,h+(n−1)​α},α=|b|.\operatorname{PF}(H)=\{h+\alpha,h+2\alpha,\ldots,h+(n-1)\alpha\},\qquad\alpha=|b|.

Then hh has a unique factorization in HH. Consequently, Conjecture 1.1 holds for HH.

Proof.

If b>0b>0, the assertion follows from Theorem 4.1. If b<0b<0, it follows from Theorem 4.2. The determinantal assertion then follows from Theorem 3.7. ∎

We now determine the defining ideal explicitly. Let S=k⁡[X1,…,Xn]S=k[X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}] be the graded polynomial ring with deg⁡Xi=si−1\deg X_{i}=s_{i-1} for all 1≤i≤n1\leq i\leq n, and set the matrix

𝖷c=(X1aX2a⋯Xn−1aXncX2X3⋯XnX1d+c+1−a).\mathsf{X}_{c}=\begin{pmatrix}X_{1}^{a}&X_{2}^{a}&\cdots&X_{n-1}^{a}&X_{n}^{c}\\ X_{2}&X_{3}&\cdots&X_{n}&X_{1}^{d+c+1-a}\end{pmatrix}.

We first verify directly, independently of the determinantal containment in [1, Remark 8.2], that I2⁡(𝖷c)⊆IH\operatorname{I}_{2}(\mathsf{X}_{c})\subseteq I_{H}. Since Ai=a​Ai−1+1A_{i}=aA_{i-1}+1, we have, for 1≤i≤n−11\leq i\leq n-1,

si\displaystyle s_{i} =m+d​Ai\displaystyle=m+dA_{i}
=m+d⁡(a​Ai−1+1)\displaystyle=m+d(aA_{i-1}+1)
=a⁡(m+d​Ai−1)+d−(a−1)​m\displaystyle=a(m+dA_{i-1})+d-(a-1)m
=a​si−1+b.\displaystyle=as_{i-1}+b.

Consequently,

(4.4) deg⁡Xi+1−deg⁡Xia=si−a​si−1=b(1≤i≤n−1).\deg X_{i+1}-\deg X_{i}^{a}=s_{i}-as_{i-1}=b\qquad(1\leq i\leq n-1).

Moreover, using m−1=c​An−1m-1=cA_{n-1}, we obtain

c​sn−1+b\displaystyle cs_{n-1}+b =c​m+c​d​An−1+b\displaystyle=cm+cdA_{n-1}+b
=c​m+d⁡(m−1)+b\displaystyle=cm+d(m-1)+b
=c​m+d​m−d+b\displaystyle=cm+dm-d+b
=(d+c)​m−(d−b)\displaystyle=(d+c)m-(d-b)
=(d+c+1−a)​m.\displaystyle=(d+c+1-a)m.

Hence

(4.5) deg⁡X1d+c+1−a−deg⁡Xnc=(d+c+1−a)​s0−c​sn−1=b.\deg X_{1}^{d+c+1-a}-\deg X_{n}^{c}=(d+c+1-a)s_{0}-cs_{n-1}=b.

Thus the difference between the weighted degrees of the bottom and top entries is the same, namely bb, in every column of 𝖷c\mathsf{X}_{c}. By Lemma 2.5, we obtain the inclusion

(4.6) I2⁡(𝖷c)⊆IH.\operatorname{I}_{2}(\mathsf{X}_{c})\subseteq I_{H}.

Notice that this argument works uniformly for both b>0b>0 and b<0b<0.

Theorem 4.4.

Under the hypotheses of Theorem 4.3, we have IH=I2⁡(𝖷c)I_{H}=\operatorname{I}_{2}(\mathsf{X}_{c}). In particular, the Eagon–Northcott complex associated to 𝖷c\mathsf{X}_{c} is the graded minimal free resolution of k⁡[H]k[H].

Proof.

The containment I2⁡(𝖷c)⊆IH\operatorname{I}_{2}(\mathsf{X}_{c})\subseteq I_{H} has already been proved in (4.6) by the weighted-degree criterion. It remains to identify the matrix supplied by Theorem 3.7.

Suppose first that b>0b>0. Then α=b\alpha=b, and Theorem 4.1 gives

h=(a−1)​s0+⋯+(a−1)​sn−2+(c−1)​sn−1.h=(a-1)s_{0}+\cdots+(a-1)s_{n-2}+(c-1)s_{n-1}.

Thus the exponents in the first row of the matrix are a,…,a,ca,\ldots,a,c. Moreover, the relations in (4.4) and (4.5) give a​si−1+b=sias_{i-1}+b=s_{i}, for all 1≤i≤n−11\leq i\leq n-1, and

c​sn−1+b=(d+c+1−a)​s0.cs_{n-1}+b=(d+c+1-a)s_{0}.

Hence the second-row exponents are 1,…,1,d+c+1−a1,\ldots,1,d+c+1-a. Therefore the matrix in Theorem 3.7 is precisely XcX_{c}.

Now suppose b<0b<0, and put α=−b\alpha=-b. By Theorem 4.2, we have that the decomposition

h=(d+c−a)​s0h=(d+c-a)s_{0}

is the unique factorization of hh. The affine relations can be rewritten as

si+α=a​si−1(1≤i≤n−1)s_{i}+\alpha=as_{i-1}\qquad(1\leq i\leq n-1)

and

(d+c+1−a)​s0+α=c​sn−1.(d+c+1-a)s_{0}+\alpha=cs_{n-1}.

Ordering the generators as s0,sn−1,sn−2,…,s1s_{0},s_{n-1},s_{n-2},\ldots,s_{1}. Theorem 3.7 yields the matrix

(X1d+c+1−aXnxn−1⋯X2XncXn−1aXn−2a⋯X1a).\begin{pmatrix}X_{1}^{d+c+1-a}&X_{n}&x_{n-1}&\cdots&X_{2}\\ X_{n}^{c}&X_{n-1}^{a}&X_{n-2}^{a}&\cdots&X_{1}^{a}\end{pmatrix}.

Interchanging its two rows and reversing the order of the columns gives exactly 𝖷c\mathsf{X}_{c}. Neither operation changes the ideal generated by the 2×22\times 2 minors. Hence IH=I2⁡(𝖷c)I_{H}=\operatorname{I}_{2}(\mathsf{X}_{c}) in both cases.

Finally, ht⁡IH=n−1\operatorname{ht}I_{H}=n-1. Since every entry of 𝖷c\mathsf{X}_{c} has positive degree, the Eagon–Northcott gives the graded minimal free resolution of k⁡[H]k[H]. ∎

Remark 4.5.

For the explicit affine family, the determinantal equality can also be checked directly. Let J=I2​(Xc)⊆IHJ=I_{2}(X_{c})\subseteq I_{H}. For a monomial matrix

M=(X1ℓ1X2ℓ2⋯XnℓnX2m2X3m3⋯X1m1)M=\begin{pmatrix}X_{1}^{\ell_{1}}&X_{2}^{\ell_{2}}&\cdots&X_{n}^{\ell_{n}}\\ X_{2}^{m_{2}}&X_{3}^{m_{3}}&\cdots&X_{1}^{m_{1}}\end{pmatrix}

of height n−1n-1, the Eagon–Northcott Hilbert series, or a count of the standard monomials modulo X1X_{1}, gives

dimkS/(I2(M)+(X1))=ℓ2⋯ℓn+m2ℓ3⋯ℓn+⋯+m2⋯mn.\dim_{k}S/(I_{2}(M)+(X_{1}))=\ell_{2}\cdots\ell_{n}+m_{2}\ell_{3}\cdots\ell_{n}+\cdots+m_{2}\cdots m_{n}.

For XcX_{c} we have (ℓ2,…,ℓn)=(a,…,a,c)(\ell_{2},\ldots,\ell_{n})=(a,\ldots,a,c) and (m2,…,mn)=(1,…,1)(m_{2},\ldots,m_{n})=(1,\ldots,1), so this length is

c​an−2+c​an−3+⋯+c​a+c+1=c​An−1+1=m.ca^{n-2}+ca^{n-3}+\cdots+ca+c+1=cA_{n-1}+1=m.

On the other hand, S/(IH+(X1))≅k⁡[H]/(tm)S/(I_{H}+(X_{1}))\cong k[H]/(t^{m}) has kk-length mm. The surjection between these Artinian quotients is therefore an isomorphism. If IH/JI_{H}/J were nonzero, it would be a nonzero finitely generated graded module over S/JS/J and would have a nonzero quotient modulo X1X_{1} by graded Nakayama, a contradiction. Thus J=IHJ=I_{H}.

This proof uses the explicit exponents of XcX_{c} and the identity m=c​An−1+1m=cA_{n-1}+1 to obtain the required length. In contrast, Theorem 3.7 constructs the cyclic relations from the pseudo-Frobenius progression and the unique factorization of hh, then supplies the ideal equality without a separate length calculation. The latter argument makes the structural reason for the determinantal presentation visible and is available whenever those two hypotheses can be verified.

We close this paper with two examples satisfying the hypotheses.

Example 4.6 (The case b>0b>0).

Take a=2a=2, n=4n=4, and c=1c=1. Then A3=1+2+4=7A_{3}=1+2+4=7 and m=A3+1=8m=A_{3}+1=8. Choose b=3b=3. Then d=(a−1)​m+b=11d=(a-1)m+b=11 and

H=⟨8,19,41,85⟩.H=\langle 8,19,41,85\rangle.

We have ρ=11​(8−1)=77\rho=11(8-1)=77, and hence

PF⁡(H)={77,74,71}={71,74,77}.\operatorname{PF}(H)=\{77,74,71\}=\{71,74,77\}.

Thus h=68h=68 and α=3\alpha=3. Theorem 4.1 gives the factorization 68=8+19+4168=8+19+41, and this is the unique factorization of 6868. The defining ideal is

IH=I2⁡(X12X22X32X4X2X3X4X111).I_{H}=\operatorname{I}_{2}\begin{pmatrix}X_{1}^{2}&X_{2}^{2}&X_{3}^{2}&X_{4}\\ X_{2}&X_{3}&X_{4}&X_{1}^{11}\end{pmatrix}.
Example 4.7 (The case b<0b<0).

Again take a=2a=2, n=4n=4, c=1c=1, and m=8m=8, but now let b=−1b=-1. Then d=7d=7 and H=⟨8,15,29,57⟩H=\langle 8,15,29,57\rangle. We have ρ=7​(8−1)=49\rho=7(8-1)=49, so

PF⁡(H)={49,50,51}.\operatorname{PF}(H)=\{49,50,51\}.

Hence h=48h=48 and α=1\alpha=1. Theorem 4.2 gives the factorization 48=6⋅848=6\cdot 8, and this is the unique factorization of 4848. The defining ideal is

IH=I2⁡(X12X22X32X4X2X3X4X17).I_{H}=\operatorname{I}_{2}\begin{pmatrix}X_{1}^{2}&X_{2}^{2}&X_{3}^{2}&X_{4}\\ X_{2}&X_{3}&X_{4}&X_{1}^{7}\end{pmatrix}.
